source: George, Walker, Monster (2019) Does Strategic Planning Improve Organizational Performance? A Meta-Analysis, Public Administration Review 79(6)
finding: Planning has a positive, small-to-moderate link to organisational performance. The effect is the answer to gap 2 (effect size).
numbers: 87 correlations from 31 studies: random-effects r = .229, 95% CI [.186,.271], I2 = 91.6%, tau2 = .032. Study-averaged (31 values): r = .255, CI [.177,.333], I2 = 91.3%. Literature search found 919 articles; 31 kept.
quote: Strategic planning ... had a significant, positive, and moderate impact on OP
limits: Public-sector focus. Very high heterogeneity. Egger test significant (bias coefficient 2.651, p<.001) but Begg not (z=1.88), so authors say publication bias cannot be ignored. Studies using multiple data sources had significantly lower effects (common-source bias). Correlational, mostly cross-sectional surveys.
agent_relevance: Planning helps on average but the effect is modest and partly inflated by single-source surveys. Use as a prior: a plan step is worth including, not worth heavy cost.

source: George, Walker, Monster (2019) moderator meta-regression (Table 2)
finding: Moderators: formal planning is strongest; participatory planning is weaker; effect is largest when performance is effectiveness and weakest for efficiency. Sector and country do not matter. The paper does NOT test environmental dynamism.
numbers: Meta-regression constant (formal planning, effectiveness, single source) = .417. Participation -.129 (p<.05). Comprehensiveness -.011 (ns). Efficiency -.357 (p<.01) vs effectiveness. Financial -.141, outcomes -.199, responsiveness -.061 (all ns). Public vs private +.068 (ns); non-US +.027 (ns). Moderators explain about 71% of variation. 10 articles on effectiveness, 5 efficiency, 15 financial.
limits: Gap 2 asked about dynamic environments: this paper has no such moderator. See d03 for that.
agent_relevance: Planning pays most for goal achievement (effectiveness), not for squeezing cost. In the scaffold, a plan should set goals and success checks, not micro-optimise steps.

source: Hamann, Halw, Guenther (2023) Corporate planning and organizational performance: a meta-analysis of contingencies, Strategic Management Journal 44(7):1803-1819 (abstract page)
finding: Larger meta-analysis. Planning-performance link holds across planning types and over time. It is larger under high environmental uncertainty, in manufacturing, in larger firms and in high uncertainty-avoidance countries.
numbers: 183 independent study samples, 84 not in earlier meta-analyses. Corrected for measurement error and dichotomisation. Numeric effect sizes were not on the abstract page (not read).
limits: Only the abstract page was opened; effect sizes and the full moderator table were not. Effects depend on how planning and performance are measured. This direction (planning matters more under uncertainty) is the opposite of the simple reading of Mintzberg.
agent_relevance: Evidence against 'planning is useless when the world is uncertain'. Supports keeping an explicit plan even in volatile tasks, and treating the plan as a tool for detecting surprise.

source: Miller and Cardinal (1994) Strategic planning and firm performance: a synthesis of more than two decades of research (AMJ); Brinckmann, Grichnik, Kapsa (2010) Should entrepreneurs plan or just storm the castle? (JBV)
finding: Metadata only. Crossref lists 603 citations for Miller and Cardinal and 521 for Brinckmann et al.; no abstract was returned and the full texts were paywalled (403/404). Effect sizes could not be verified.
numbers: Crossref citation counts only: 603 (Miller and Cardinal), 521 (Brinckmann et al.), 228 (Brews and Hunt 1999).
limits: Not read. Do not quote effect sizes from memory.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays partly open: the older meta-analyses were not opened.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella, Spina (2020) A Scientific Approach to Entrepreneurial Decision Making: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial, Management Science (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Randomised trial. Startups taught to form hypotheses and run tests (a scientific approach) did better, pivoted more, and did not drop out more than controls. Both arms got 10 sessions of general training.
numbers: 116 Italian startups, 16 data points over about one year. Treated vs control. The abstract gives no revenue effect size; the numeric effects were not seen.
quote: entrepreneurs who behave like scientists perform better, are more likely to pivot to a different idea, and are not more likely to drop out
limits: Abstract only; the effect sizes need the full paper. Small N, one country, one training programme. Theory claim: a scientific approach raises precision (fewer false-positive projects kept, more false-negatives revived).
agent_relevance: A hypothesis-and-test loop beats intuition for strategy-like choices. Fits S9: write the hypothesis behind a plan, test it, pivot on the result.

source: Koning, Hasan, Chatterji (2022) Experimentation and startup performance: Evidence from A/B testing (NBER w26278 / SSRN 3440291 abstracts)
finding: Startups adopting A/B testing showed higher page views and more product launches, robust to instrumental variables and synthetic control using Google's tool launch. Testers try big changes, and scale or fail faster.
numbers: Abstract gives no N and no effect size ('large sample of high-technology startups'). Few firms adopt. Experienced managers gain more.
limits: Abstract only; numbers not seen. Observational with IV and synthetic control, not randomised.
agent_relevance: Experiments raise the variance of outcomes (both tails). For the agent: cheap tests are useful, but need a rule to stop failing branches early.

source: Mintzberg and Waters (1985) Of strategies, deliberate and emergent, Strategic Management Journal 6(3) (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Abstract confirms: deliberate and emergent are two ends of a continuum; the paper elaborates eight types: planned, entrepreneurial, ideological, umbrella, process, unconnected, consensus, imposed. Crossref lists 3,027 citations.
numbers: 8 types named. Full text (how deliberateness is measured, the case data) was blocked by the publisher (HTTP 403), so gap 5 is only partly closed.
quote: Deliberate and emergent strategies may be conceived as two ends of a continuum along which real-world strategies lie.
limits: Abstract only. Do not attribute a measurement procedure to the paper without the text.
agent_relevance: Types give a vocabulary for the agent's plan state: planned (fully intended), umbrella (broad guardrails, detail left open), process (method set, content left open). Umbrella is the closest match to a scaffold that sets guardrails G1-G12 and leaves moves open.

source: Romasanta, Thomas, Levina (2026) Researchers asked LLMs for strategic advice; they got 'trendslop' (Harvard Business Review, March 2026), via web-search summary
finding: Search summary: across seven business tensions LLMs favoured differentiation over commoditisation, augmentation over automation, and long-term over short-term, regardless of company context or prompt style. Richer context and better prompts helped little. When not forced to choose, models often said do everything at once.
numbers: Seven tensions. A secondary commentary says even rich context moved the bias by only about 11 percent; that figure was NOT verified against the original.
limits: Only the search-engine summary was seen; the HBR article was not opened. Numbers from the original are not available.
agent_relevance: Strategic advice from an LLM has a fashion bias. The scaffold should force a stated counter-case and a forced-choice step before an advice-like recommendation.

source: Lerer (2026) Strategy Trendslop as Parasitic Spontaneous Order (Zenodo working paper, April 2026), record page
finding: Pilot replication of trendslop with two models. GPT-4o is strongly context-sensitive and complies with adversarial instructions; Claude Sonnet 4.5 resists.
numbers: 240 runs, 4 tensions, 3 prompt variants, pre-registered on GitHub. Non-compliance with direct adversarial instruction: Claude Sonnet 75.0% vs GPT-4o 27.5%. GPT-4o with specific context: 98% Direct vs 72% under generic prompt (a full reversal).
limits: Working paper, not peer reviewed, single author. Record page only; per-tension percentages and mitigation numbers not on the page.
agent_relevance: Context can flip the bias in some models and not others, so test any prompt fix per model.

source: Chen, Narasimhan, Liu (2026) CEO-Bench: Can Agents Play the Long Game? (arXiv 2606.18543)
finding: 500-day simulated startup, partially observable and noisy. Only three evaluated models end above the $1M start in their best run; every model is below a rule-based baseline.
numbers: Three runs per model (best run reported). Best-run final cash: rule-based baseline $15.8M; Claude Fable 5 $12.6M; GPT-5.6 Sol $11.3M; Claude Opus 4.8 $2.4M; Qwen 3.7 Max $365.3k; others $33k-$75k. GPT-5.6 Sol's other two runs went bankrupt near day 190. DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok 4.20 bankrupt on all runs. With the horizon cut to 50 days, no model finishes above start cash.
limits: Best-of-three selection flatters models; run-to-run spread is large.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 7 in part: multiple runs per setting exist, and run spread is as large as the gap between models. Report mean and worst run, not best.

source: CEO-Bench (Chen et al. 2026) planning and memo analysis, sections 3.2-3.3
finding: Harness clears action history each simulated week and keeps only an agent-editable memory file. Top agents keep revising a written plan and write if-then contingencies. Opus 4.8 harvested after early growth; Fable 5 kept revising its plan late.
numbers: Targeted R&D share of development dollars: Fable 5 88%, Opus 4.8 51%, Qwen 3.7 Max 25%, GLM 5.1 19%, Grok 4.20 11%. Planning proxy: frequency of the word if in memos, higher for Fable 5 and Opus 4.8.
limits: Correlational; proxy for planning is a word count. No ablation that removes the plan memo.
agent_relevance: Closest real match to the Mintzberg gap: a plan file edited every week with contingencies. Not a controlled test of diffing plan against trace, so gap 1 stays open.

source: OPPO AI Agent Team (2026) EcoGym (arXiv 2602.09514v3), results and ablations
finding: No model wins all three economies. Vending is high-variance (5 runs averaged); Freelance and Operation use 3 runs. Memory helps but not always; best memory type depends on model and task. Thinking on helped both Gemini models in Operation.
numbers: Operation DAU, Gemini-3-Flash: 1194 without thinking, 1396 with. 3 human experts average DAU 1404; Claude-Sonnet-4.5 beat it. Memory ablation, Gemini-3-Pro: none 11282, working 13679, symbolic 15567, episodic 18939, Mem0 15406; Gemini-3-Flash none 5676, working 10099. Context 32 to 1024 gave no consistent gain.
limits: Environment label of the memory table unclear in extracted text. Human baseline: 3 people, 15 min familiarisation, one environment.
agent_relevance: Model-dependent effects mean the scaffold must be tested on at least two models. Episodic notes gave the biggest lift for the stronger model.

source: Dai, Peng, Qian, Xie (2026) Can LLMs Be CEOs? Benchmarking Strategic Resource Reallocation with Multi-Role Agent Simulation (arXiv 2606.17459)
finding: Five models, 13 scenarios, four advisor roles. All produce valid plans but differ in calibration of boldness. Failure modes: single-advisor capture, conservative default under ambiguity, historical amnesia. Models that engage more with conflicting views act less decisively.
numbers: Overall: Gemma-4-27B 73.86, GPT-OSS-20B 71.90, Qwen-Plus 67.17, Claude-3.5-Haiku 65.82, Nemotron-9B 63.87. Valid plans 13/13, 13/13, 12/13, 11/13, 11/13. Temperature 0.2, each model run ONCE per scenario.
limits: Single run per scenario, LLM-judged rubric, small models. Does not answer gap 7 about multi-run differences.
agent_relevance: The integration versus boldness tradeoff mirrors planned versus emergent: deliberation over conflict lowers decisiveness. The scaffold needs a commit rule after a bounded number of views.

source: Yang et al. (2026) EnterpriseBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Enterprise-Level Strategic Reasoning and Decision-Making (arXiv 2609.37658)
finding: Nine agent methods, four backbones. The best method changes with task and backbone. Reflexion and Self-Refine stay below plain CoT in consulting cases. No method is stable across tasks.
numbers: Beer Game cost under DeepSeek-V3: Discussion lowest at 1.94e4; under GPT-4.1 best is GEPA and Discussion is much worse. EDT earnings: AMEM 6.76M (DeepSeek-V3) vs GEPA 8.16M (GPT-4.1). Consulting: GEPA 8.28 (DeepSeek-V3); DC 8.08 vs GEPA 7.89 (GPT-4.1). LLM judge vs humans r = 0.71 (20 cases) and 0.887 (100 cases, 500 transcripts).
limits: Number of repeated runs per cell not found in the text read. Rankings flip across backbones.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 6 in part: reflection memory does not reliably help on vague, rubric-judged strategy tasks. S9 learning needs a checker.

source: Sun et al. (2023) AdaPlanner: Adaptive Planning from Feedback with Language Models (arXiv 2305.16653)
finding: Closed-loop planning with an explicit plan and predicted observations. Matching observations are folded in (in-plan refinement); a mismatch triggers plan rewriting (out-of-plan refinement). A working diff-plan-against-reality, replan-on-surprise design (gaps 1 and 3).
numbers: ALFWorld overall success 91.79% (GPT-3) and 80.60% (gpt-3.5-turbo); MiniWoB++ 91.11% with feedback. Claimed +3.73% over best baseline with 2x fewer samples. Without code-style interface (GPT-3.5): ALFWorld 81% to 46%, MiniWoB++ 93% to 66%.
limits: No comparison of replan-every-step vs replan-on-surprise at equal tokens. Old models. Demonstration counts differ across baselines.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 equal-token test stays open, but the trigger is clear: replan when an observation contradicts the plan's prediction. Easy to log in our scaffold.

source: Sun et al. (2023) AdaPlanner skill discovery ablation (Fig. 4d)
finding: Storing successful plans as skills reused as few-shot exemplars nearly doubles ALFWorld success and adds about 15 points on MiniWoB++. Nearest LLM test of promoting an execution success into the plan (gap 4).
numbers: ALFWorld: nearly doubles with skill discovery (one demonstration of the simplest task, scored on the five harder tasks, GPT-3.5). MiniWoB++: about +15% overall. Exact bar values not cleanly extracted.
limits: One round of skill discovery, one model, text environments with a verifier. Not a business strategy setting.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 closed in part: promoting verified successes into the plan helps when a hard success signal exists.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.01798)
finding: Reflection helps only when given the true answer. Without oracle labels, intrinsic self-correction does not improve and often hurts.
numbers: GPT-3.5 with oracle labels: GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 82.0, HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0 (GPT-4 oracle: 97.5, 85.5, 59.0). Intrinsic, no oracle: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8 (round 2); GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 and 74.7; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Reasoning tasks, 2023 models; later work shows fine-tuning changes this.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 6: reflection needs a hard verifier. For strategy tasks without one, tie S9 notes to an external check or observed outcome.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction (arXiv 2406.01297)
finding: No prior work shows successful self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback, except on tasks exceptionally suited to it. Self-correction works where reliable external feedback exists. Large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
numbers: Three qualitative conclusions; no pooled effect size.
limits: Survey, not a new experiment. Abstract and introduction read; full tables not checked.
agent_relevance: Confirms gap 6: vague feedback on strategy-like tasks is the weak case. Put external checks in the S9 loop.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (arXiv 2308.10144v3)
finding: Cross-task insight memory from success and failure pairs. Insights alone or retrieval alone is worse than both. Insights from the few-shot examples alone give no gain over ReAct. Adding reflections to insight extraction hurt, possibly through hallucinated reflections. Learned insights beat hand-crafted ones.
numbers: HotpotQA: ExpeL 40% vs Reflexion 39%; ALFWorld: ExpeL 54% vs Reflexion 59% (Reflexion used retries, ExpeL did not). Insights-only 37% vs retrieve-only 38% on one setting.
limits: Deterministic text environments with success/failure signals. Differences are small versus standard error.
agent_relevance: Supports gaps 6 and 4: lessons promoted from real experience beat hand-written ones; unverified reflections can poison memory.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (arXiv 2409.07429), abstract
finding: Agents induce reusable workflows from past successful runs and reuse them. Gains on web tasks; online induction generalises across tasks, sites and domains.
numbers: Relative success +24.6% on Mind2Web and +51.1% on WebArena, fewer steps on WebArena; online AWM beats baselines by 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as the train-test gap widens.
limits: Abstract read; tables not checked. Web navigation with task checks.
agent_relevance: Second LLM instance of promoting emergent successes into a standing routine (gap 4). Suggests promoting a pattern only after it repeats.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation (arXiv 2505.06120)
finding: Models make early assumptions, give a final answer too soon, then rely on it and do not recover. This is plan momentum in LLMs (gap 10).
numbers: Average drop 39% single-turn to multi-turn across six tasks, 15 models, 200,000+ simulated conversations. Aptitude loss about 15%, unreliability up 112%. Temperature 0 did not fix reliability in the tested settings. Two or more shards already trigger the effect.
limits: Underspecified chat tasks, not strategy tasks. Simulated user.
agent_relevance: After new information arrives, restart from a recap rather than extending the earlier draft. The outside-signal trigger should reset, not patch.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST, arXiv 2503.13657v3)
finding: Failure taxonomy of 14 modes in 3 groups. Several are plan-action drift: step repetition, unaware of termination, reasoning-action mismatch, premature termination, incomplete verification.
numbers: 1600+ annotated traces, 7 frameworks, kappa = 0.88 on 150 traces. Rough shares: reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, unaware of termination 12.4%, disobey task specification 11.8%.
limits: Percentages differ between table versions in the PDF text; use as rough order only. Multi-agent frameworks.
agent_relevance: A checklist of drift modes to log when diffing intended plan against the action trace (gap 1). No test that diffing improves score.
